synopsis: ASME V&V 10 covers structural models, V&V 20 fluid-flow and heat-transfer models, and V&V 40 risk-based credibility for medical-device models; the booklet relies most on V&V 40 (2018), interpreted through FDA guidance dated November 2023 [f14616, f14620, f14624, f8072]. V&V 40 ties credibility to a stated context of use and model risk—model influence combined with decision consequence—with credibility goals set prospectively; it prescribes neither a universal acceptance error nor a universal minimum amount of physical evidence [f14621, f14622, f8075, f7790, f8076]. Across the planning and review chapters, ASME and NASA support validation against the real application, rather than internal consistency or simulation run count alone [f9454, f10755, f10884]. The booklet rates V&V 40 and FDA guidance as the most transferable reasoning framework for off-road automatic braking, but they are not proven for that application, and no direct equivalent framework was found for earth-moving-machine automatic braking [f8077, f8078, f7740]. Their scope is physics-based models: vehicle dynamics and brakes can use this framework, while machine-learned perception needs separate assurance; V&V 10 and V&V 20 were named but not verified in the research [f14627, f14623].
